title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: P is a prime and we look at solutions x, taken mod P (so 0 < x < P), of x^n ≡ 1 (mod P). The previous page states that when n divides P−1 the congruence has exactly n solutions. Definition §30: a 'proper case' (casus proprius) of x^n − 1 is a solution that solves no x^m − 1 with m < n. In modern terms this is a residue of exact multiplicative order n, i.e. a primitive n-th root of unity mod P.

- §31 (Coroll. 1): x = 1 solves every x^m − 1, so it is never proper. Hence the number of proper cases is at most n − 1.
- §32 (Coroll. 2): if n is prime, the only lower exponent dividing n is 1. So there are n − 1 proper cases, which is φ(n) for prime n.
- §33 (Coroll. 3): if n = μν, then x^μ − 1 and x^ν − 1 divide x^n − 1. Their solutions are therefore solutions of x^n − 1 and must be removed when counting proper cases.
- §34 (Problema): for every n, find the number of proper cases. The solution on the next page uses recursive inclusion–exclusion over the divisors of n: N(n) = n − Σ_{d|n, d<n} N(d). This produces the table 1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 2, 6, 4, 6, i.e. Euler's totient φ(n), via Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n.

Purpose: this count is the core of Euler's argument that primitive roots mod P exist. Since x^{P−1} − 1 has P − 1 solutions, the proper cases for n = P − 1 number φ(P − 1) > 0.
errors: §31 says the total number of cases is n without qualification. That is true only when n divides P − 1. In general the count is gcd(n, P − 1), as the previous page itself concedes when it calls some solutions 'impossible/imaginary'. So the corollaries tacitly assume n | P − 1.

§33 is loosely phrased. It says x^n − 1 is divisible 'in the same cases' as x^μ − 1 and x^ν − 1; it should say that their cases are contained among its cases. Moreover, for a general composite n, removing only the cases of x^μ − 1 and x^ν − 1 for one factorization misses other divisors (e.g. n = 12). This is repaired on the next page by excluding the proper cases of every divisor.

The claim that x^n − 1 has exactly n roots mod P when n | P − 1 rests on the root-count bound for polynomial congruences mod P (at most deg roots). Euler uses this bound; its rigorous status in his era is the classical gap discussed in histories (Lagrange 1768/70 gave the bound).

ideas.what: Definition of 'proper cases' of x^n ≡ 1 (mod P): residues of exact order n
ideas.modern_name: elements of multiplicative order n / primitive n-th roots of unity mod p
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (order concept, E262, E449); systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones (1801), §§52–55
ideas.where_published: E449 (Novi Comm. 18, 1774); related ideas in E262

ideas.what: Number of proper cases is n − 1 for prime n, and is obtained by subtracting the proper cases of the divisors for composite n
ideas.modern_name: Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n; number of elements of order d in a cyclic group equals φ(d)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones §39 and §§52–55; Euler E449 is recognized as an earlier (gappy) version
ideas.where_published: E449; discussed by Weil, Number Theory: An Approach through History; Sandifer, How Euler Did It

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known setup of Euler's 1774 primitive-root argument, which is discussed in the standard histories (Weil, Sandifer, Gauss's own remarks). The corollaries are elementary and already credited.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image; only minor typography (long s retained). In §32 the image reads 'x^1 − 1' (the printed exponent looks like an apostrophe), as transcribed.
